description: Somos Constanza Ficco, Santiago Aguilera, Lucas Porzio and Felipe Bollinger. Tenemos una cualidad en común: buscar soluciones a los problemas de una manera creativa y funcional. Cada uno cuenta con capacidades diferentes, como las matemáticas, la tecnología, el medio ambiente, la agricultura, electrónica, pensamiento crítico, analisis de información entre otras.
summary: One wrong landing site can end a mission before it starts. And choosing one means decoding data most people can't read. At the lunar South Pole, some areas never get sunlight, and mountains block communications with Earth. That's why we invented LuNav: an interactive web tool using real satellite images of the South Pole to compare landing sites and dates. Click any point, and our copilot, Belisario, tells you: Is there sunlight? Can you communicate with Earth? The future of exploration in one click. And it starts with LuNav.
details:
LuNav (Lunar Landing Site Navigator) is an interactive mission planning and selenographic simulation platform designed to evaluate landing sites across the Lunar South Pole (-85° to -90° latitude).

How It Works & Key Features: Planning a mission to the Lunar South Pole requires balancing two critical constraints: harvesting solar energy where the Sun never rises more than ~1.54° above the ideal horizon at the pole, and maintaining Direct-to-Earth (DTE) radio communication as Earth oscillates across the sky due to optical librations. LuNav solves this through three synchronized modules: • 2D & 3D Topographic Exploration: Users can select Artemis candidate landing sites (Shackleton Rim, Connecting Ridge, Malapert Mountain, Haworth Rim) or click any coordinate on a 2D polar stereographic map, then switch to an expanded 3D terrain explorer (Lunar Window 3D) built with real NASA LOLA elevation models and LROC imagery, featuring both orbital and first-person surface ("Lunar Street View") navigation. • Topocentric Selenographic Physics Engine: Powered by NASA/JPL Horizons and SPICE (DE440s / IAU_MOON) orbital mechanics, LuNav computes real-time elevation and azimuth angles for the Sun and Earth at any UTC timestamp, modeling the Moon's 346.6-day seasonal cycle, optical librations, and local horizon terrain masking (0°–10°). • 30-Day Window & Scenario Comparator: A 30-day timeline simulator calculates the percentage of time a site simultaneously achieves sunlight and a viable Direct-to-Earth link (≥ 5° elevation). Users can pin multiple site, date, and terrain combinations into a side-by-side comparison table to evaluate mission viability.

Benefits, Impact & Creativity: LuNav bridges professional mission design and STEM education by making complex astrodynamics accessible in the browser. It blends rigorous aerospace calculations with Argentine spaceflight heritage and retro pixel-art storytelling: the user's copilot is Belisario, inspired by the real mouse launched by Argentina on April 11, 1967, from Chamical, La Rioja. Alongside a custom WebGL flaming Sol de Mayo intro and a live horizon plane showing Belisario tracking the Sun and Earth over local crater rims, LuNav includes a Simple/Technical Mode toggle, bilingual support (EN/ES), and a built-in Teacher Guide with three interactive classroom challenges.

Tools, Languages & Data Used: • Frontend & 3D Graphics: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+), Three.js, custom WebGL GLSL shaders, and HTML5 2D Canvas. • Backend & Ephemerides: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, SpiceyPy, and a client-side JavaScript ephemeris engine. • NASA Datasets: LRO LOLA South Pole Digital Elevation Models (DEM), LROC Wide Angle Camera (WAC) surface textures (IAU:30135 projection), and NASA/JPL SPICE kernels (de440s.bsp, pck00011.tpc, naif0012.tls). • Deployment: Git, GitHub, and Vercel.
